evidence.excerpt: When a job shop produces several product families simultaneously, interactions between queues complicate capacity and pricing analysis. This paper applies decomposition-based queueing network approximations (specifically the parametric decomposition method) to a three-product job shop, where each product's arrival rate is a decreasing linear function of its posted price. A profit-maximising price vector is found by gradient search over the resulting approximate steady-state performance functions. The model is validated against simulation on test instances constructed to match characteristics of a Novi Sad sheet-metal fabrication plant. Approximation errors in throughput and mean waiting time are below 8% across a wide range of utilisation levels. The optimal price vector under the approximate model achieves within 3% of the simulation-optimal revenue. A key finding is that ignoring the queueing interaction between product classes overstates optimal prices by 6–12% at high utilisation, with implications for firms quoting jobs without workload visibility across product lines.
